key_insight: Machine-learned long-timescale simulations show that small polarons at reduced rutile TiO2(110) surfaces move far less than in bulk because surface geometry removes many efficient hopping routes.
engineering_relevance: This helps explain why porous rutile TiO2 can have much lower electron mobility than single-crystal material, which matters for catalysis, photovoltaics, batteries, and other oxide-device applications.
method: Extend machine-learning-assisted polaron dynamics to a redox-active oxide surface (oxygen-deficient rutile TiO2(110)).
Run nanosecond-scale simulations across temperatures to sample rare polaron hops.
Analyze site occupancy and hopping pathways near oxygen vacancies and surface layers.
evidence_signal: The study reports several nanoseconds of temperature-dependent dynamics, showing surface polaron mobility is suppressed by orders of magnitude relative to bulk and that vacancies bias charge localization near nearby Ti sites.
watch_item: The approach is demonstrated on a paradigmatic oxide surface, so transferability to other materials may still require retraining and careful validation of the learned dynamics.
paper_title: Machine-learned dynamics of surface polarons at reduced oxide surfaces
